title: What are stream characteristics / Spliterator flags (ORDERED, SIZED, SORTED, DISTINCT, NONNULL, IMMUTABLE, CONCURRENT), and how do they let the pipeline optimize?
shortTitle: Spliterator characteristics/flags — ORDERED, SIZED, SORTED, DISTINCT and pipeline optimization
topicTitle: What are stream characteristics / Spliterator flags

s1_definition.profdef: Spliterator characteristics are bit flags that describe properties of the stream source. The stream pipeline uses them to OPTIMIZE execution: `SIZED` enables pre-allocated result containers (ArrayList of exact size). `ORDERED` ensures encounter order is preserved — absence allows forEach to run unordered in parallel. `SORTED` lets sorted() become a no-op if the source is already sorted. `DISTINCT` lets distinct() become a no-op if elements are already unique. `NONNULL` means no null elements. `IMMUTABLE` means the source won't be modified during traversal. `CONCURRENT` means the source supports concurrent modification safely.
s1_definition.analogy: The conveyor belt has LABELS: "SORTED by amount" (SORTED), "exactly 100 items" (SIZED), "all unique" (DISTINCT). If the belt is labeled SORTED and you ask to sort it — skip! Already done. If labeled SIZED, the packing machine pre-cuts a box of exactly 100 slots. These labels let the factory SKIP unnecessary work.
s1_definition.oneliner: SIZED = pre-allocate. ORDERED = preserve order. SORTED = skip sort. DISTINCT = skip distinct. Flags enable the pipeline to skip redundant operations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spliterator characteristics are bit flags that describe properties of the stream source. The stream pipeline uses them to OPTIMIZE execution: `SIZED` enables pre-allocated result containers (ArrayList of exact size). `ORDERED` ensures encounter order is preserved — absence allows forEach to run unordered in parallel. `SORTED` lets sorted() become a no-op if the source is already sorted. `DISTINCT` lets distinct() become a no-op if elements are already unique. `NONNULL` means no null elements. `IMMUTABLE` means the source won't be modified during traversal. `CONCURRENT` means the source supports concurrent modification safely.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The conveyor belt has LABELS: "SORTED by amount" (SORTED), "exactly 100 items" (SIZED), "all unique" (DISTINCT). If the belt is labeled SORTED and you ask to sort it — skip! Already done. If labeled SIZED, the packing machine pre-cuts a box of exactly 100 slots. These labels let the factory SKIP unnecessary work.

**One line to remember:** SIZED = pre-allocate. ORDERED = preserve order. SORTED = skip sort. DISTINCT = skip distinct. Flags enable the pipeline to skip redundant operations.

sections.s2_technical:
A `Spliterator` is the engine under every stream: it both describes how to traverse elements (`tryAdvance`) and how to split them for parallelism (`trySplit`). Its CHARACTERISTICS are bit flags that let the stream pipeline optimise. Key flags: `ORDERED` (elements have a meaningful encounter order), `SIZED` (the exact count is known up front), `SORTED` (already sorted by some comparator), `DISTINCT` (no duplicates), `NONNULL`, and `IMMUTABLE`/`CONCURRENT`.

These flags drive optimisations. If a source is `SIZED`, the pipeline can pre-allocate the result array and even skip a `peek` whose output is unused for `count()`. If it is already `SORTED` with the right comparator, `sorted()` becomes a no-op. If it is `DISTINCT`, a later `distinct()` can be skipped. An `ArrayList` spliterator is `ORDERED` and `SIZED` and splits cheaply (great for parallel); a `HashSet` is `DISTINCT` but not `ORDERED`; a `LinkedList` splits poorly.

A banking example: streaming an `ArrayList` of trades in parallel is efficient because its spliterator is `SIZED` and splits in O(1), while the same over a `LinkedList` is slow. Senior nuance: choose the source collection for the stream workload — array-backed sources give `SIZED`/`ORDERED` spliterators that parallelise and optimise well; understanding characteristics explains why `sorted()`/`distinct()` sometimes cost nothing and why parallel speedups depend on the source.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — A parallel trade aggregation was slow because it streamed a `LinkedList`, whose spliterator splits poorly and is not SIZED, defeating parallelism. Fix: back the data with an `ArrayList`, whose spliterator reports SIZED/ORDERED and splits in O(1), so the parallel pipeline can pre-size results and balance work across cores.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: an array-backed list [10, 20, 30].

**Step 2.** `list.spliterator()` exposes the traversal/splitting engine with its characteristic flags.

**Step 3.** The spliterator reports `SIZED`, so the exact count (3) is known and the pipeline can pre-allocate results.

**Step 4.** It reports `ORDERED`, so encounter order is preserved and operations like `findFirst` are deterministic.

**Step 5.** These flags let parallel streams split cheaply and skip redundant `sorted`/`distinct` when already satisfied.

```text
INFO: SIZED=true ORDERED=true estimateSize=3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  List [10, 20, 30]  →  spliterator()
    │ characteristics (bit flags):
    ├─ SIZED    → exact count known → pre-allocate, skip some ops
    ├─ ORDERED  → encounter order kept → findFirst deterministic
    ├─ DISTINCT → later distinct() can be skipped
    └─ SORTED   → later sorted() becomes no-op
  ArrayList: SIZED+ORDERED, splits O(1) (great parallel)
  LinkedList: splits poorly (bad parallel)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spliterator characteristics are optimization hints that the stream pipeline reads before execution. SIZED means the element count is known — the pipeline pre-allocates result containers of exact size. SORTED means elements are already sorted — sorted() becomes a no-op. DISTINCT means elements are unique — distinct() becomes a no-op. ORDERED means encounter order matters — the pipeline must preserve it. Absence of ORDERED allows parallel forEach to skip coordination. These flags are why `treeSet.stream().sorted()` is instant (source is already SORTED) while `arrayList.stream().sorted()` buffers all elements.
